source: Widyasari et al. (2024) FuseFL: Demystifying Faulty Code with LLM (prompt ablation)
finding: An Ochiai suspiciousness list put in the prompt (SusScore) helps ChatGPT only a little over plain chain-of-thought, and helps far less than the failing-test result. Combining them helps more.
numbers: 324 faulty student Python programs (600 faulty lines), GPT-3.5. Top-1 faults found: Ochiai alone about 117; baseline prompt 150; CoT 163; SusScore (top-5 Ochiai lines) 169; TestRes (test results) 187; SusScore+TestRes 192; all inputs (FuseFL) 197. SusScore is +3.7% over CoT at Top-1 but +44% over Ochiai alone. Top-3: SusScore 257 (highest single input), TestRes 242.
limits: Student programs, short files, one model, no token matching (longer prompts). The Top-1 row of Table IV was read from garbled PDF text; the paper text confirms SusScore +3.7% over CoT and TestRes best at Top-1 and Top-2. Not an agent loop.
agent_relevance: Direct (non-agent) evidence for Gap 1: a spectrum hint adds a small gain at Top-1 and mostly helps ranking depth. Test results matter more. Treat Ochiai as a weak extra, not a core step.
quote: In 77 cases where SBFL failed at Top-3, only 8 were localized at Top-1 using the SusScore prompt

source: Farzandway and Ghassemi (2025) Automated Repair of C Programs Using LLMs
finding: On Codeflaws, adding Ochiai suspiciousness (lines with score above 0.5) to the prompt raised repair accuracy in every model and in both single-query and iterative settings, by a few points each.
numbers: 3,902 bugs. Llama 3.1 405b: test results only 36.80% -> plus SBFL 41.13% (single query); chain-of-thought loop 42.92% -> with SBFL 44.93%. Llama 3.2 90b: 27.22->30.22 and 34.09->38.13. Llama 3.1 70b: 27.93->30.24 and 38.39->38.83. No feedback at all: 29.01%/22.42%/21.76%. GPT-4 CoT baseline 41.32%.
limits: Small C student-style programs. Gains are 0.4 to 4.3 points, from one run each, no confidence intervals, no token-matched control (the iterative loops took about 80 s vs about 17 s). Not a published ablation of SBFL alone at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Best available answer to Gap 1: the hint helps a little (about +3 points single query, +2.4 iterative) and never hurt here. Still no equal-token test and no agent on real repos.

source: Ramos, Mamede, Jain et al. (2025) Are Large Language Models Memorizing Bug Benchmarks?
finding: Defects4J is the bug benchmark most likely to be memorised. Some older code models reproduce its solution files nearly verbatim. Newer large models show far less sign.
numbers: Defects4J: 80% of its repositories are in TheStack training data (v1.0, 2.0, 2.1); SWE-bench Lite 83.3-91.7%; GitBug-Java 38.9-61.1%. codegen-multi 6B: NLL 0.15 on Defects4J, 82% 5-gram accuracy; CodeLlama 7B and Gemma-2 27B 64% 5-gram accuracy. LLaMa 3.1 70B: NLL ratio Defects4J vs GitBug-Java only 1.27 (little leakage signal). Defects4J had the lowest NLL of all benchmarks across models.
limits: Measures familiarity with the patch file in base models (NLL, n-gram). It does not measure localisation accuracy directly. Instruction-tuned and closed models were not tested for n-gram accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: leakage risk for Defects4J-based localisation numbers is real for older and mid-size open models, less clear for frontier models. Use post-cutoff or renamed bugs for our own evaluations.
quote: Defects4J consistently exhibits the highest rate of potential memorization

source: De Koning, Asgari, Derakhshanfar, Panichella (2026) Metamorphic testing to diagnose memorization in LLM program repair
finding: Renaming identifiers and other meaning-preserving edits cut repair success on Defects4J for all seven LLMs. The size of the drop tracks how familiar the original bug was (low NLL).
numbers: Defects4J, function-level location given (not the exact line). Success rate drop after transformation: Claude-3.7 77.31%->72.42% (-4.89), GPT-4o 65.93->61.92 (-4.01), GPT-4o-mini 57.17->51.36 (-5.81), Gemma-2-27B 44.38->36.07 (-8.31), Llama-3.1 35.08->19.11 (-15.98), Ministral-7B -6.91, StarCoder2 -7.78; all p<0.001. GitBug-Java (post-cutoff): no significant drop for Claude-3.7 (+0.27, p=0.819) and GPT-4o (+1.76, p=0.667); GPT-4o-mini -8.67 (p=0.074). Spearman of NLL with drop: Gemma-2 0.303, Llama-3.1 0.165, Mistral-7B 0.218.
limits: Tests repair, not localisation. Only solvable bugs counted. Small correlations. Transformations may also add real brittleness, not only leakage.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed for repair: Defects4J scores are inflated by 4 to 16 points. A localisation-specific mutated-identifier test is still missing.

source: Meng et al. (2025) LLM-based Agents for Automated Bug Fixing: How Far Are We?
finding: Six top SWE-bench Verified systems: file-level localisation tracks resolve rate, but a system with weak localisation can still repair well when its localisation hits.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified, 500 issues. W&B Programmer localized at least one buggy file in 448 cases, all buggy files in 394; Learn-by-interact 342 (W&B +31.0%). Given a file hit, resolve probability 281/342=82.2% (Learn-by-interact) vs 69.6% (W&B Programmer); symbol-level 85.1% vs 72.7%. 404 issues solved by at least one tool, 96 by none, 181 by all six.
limits: Localisation was inferred from the final patch, not from intermediate search. Six systems, single runs.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: file-level localisation is largely solved; the remaining failures are symbol-level localisation and repair. Localisation accuracy is necessary, not sufficient.

source: Meng et al. (2025) issue-quality analysis (same paper, RQ1)
finding: Issues no tool could solve differ from issues all tools solved mostly in the quality of the proposed solution in the report, not in location hints or reproduction examples.
numbers: Mean score ratio, all-solved set (181 issues) over none-solved set (96): solution quality 1.95x; symbol-level location 1.30x; file-level 1.26x; line-level 1.22x; reproducible example 1.01x.
limits: Scores come from an LLM judge validated against human annotation; correlational. Test-based fault localisation (spectrum, mutation) was unusable because the protocol forbids running the hidden tests.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: bug-report content strongly shapes success. A report that names the cause helps most. Reports that only show a symptom are the hard cases.

source: Cuadron et al. (2025) The Danger of Overthinking: Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks
finding: In SWE-bench Verified agent runs, more overthinking (planning in place of acting on feedback) goes with fewer resolved issues. Reasoning models overthink about three times as much as non-reasoning ones.
numbers: 4,018 trajectories scored 0-10 by an LLM judge. Regression slopes: reasoning models -7.894, non-reasoning -15.938 resolution points per overthinking point. o1 high effort 29.1% resolved at $1,400; o1 low effort 21.0% at $400. Choosing the lower-overthinking sample gave about +30% resolution and -43% cost.
limits: LLM-judge score, correlational, one scaffold (CodeAct/OpenHands). Concerns acting vs planning, not specifically over-checking after the fault is found.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: over-thinking is measured; premature stopping is also a named failure. A stop rule needs both a verify trigger and a cap. The overthinking score may be a cheap gate for choosing among samples.
quote: Analysis Paralysis, Rogue Actions, and Premature Disengagement

source: Bouzenia and Pradel (2025) Understanding Software Engineering Agents: Thought-Action-Result Trajectories
finding: Failing agent runs are longer and show repeated identical actions, fixes written without testing, and stopping with no valid test.
numbers: 120 trajectories (RepairAgent, AutoCodeRover, OpenHands; 2,822 LLM calls). Mean length RepairAgent 34 iterations (failed 40 vs fixed 22), OpenHands 29, AutoCodeRover 6. Mean tokens: AutoCodeRover 23K, RepairAgent 220K, OpenHands 1.2M (52x ACR). Three anti-patterns named: repeated identical actions, consecutive fixes without tests, termination without proper validation.
limits: Qualitative coding on 40 sampled trajectories per agent; different benchmarks per agent (Defects4J vs SWE-bench Lite).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 6: agents both under-verify (stop without a valid test) and loop (repeat searches). Supports a verify-once-then-stop rule plus a repeat-action detector.
quote: Robust agents design should include checks for anti-patterns and trajectory smells.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) AutoSD, Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging
finding: The hypothesis-then-experiment prompt did not beat plainly asking for the fix. It matches it and adds an explanation.
numbers: Correct patches: Defects4J v1.2 LLM-Base 87 vs AutoSD 76; v2.0 110 vs 113. ARHE (200 mutated HumanEval bugs): plausible 179 vs 189, correct 177 vs 187. 10 candidates per bug. Developer study (20 participants): review time not significantly different with explanations.
limits: Same 10-sample budget, not equal tokens (AutoSD uses more calls). Function-level fault location is given. ChatGPT-era model.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: with real execution, hypothesis-experiment gives no clear repair-accuracy gain over plain prompting here. Its value is the explanation and the confidence flag, not accuracy.

source: Kang et al. AutoSD debugger ablation and DONE token (RQ2)
finding: Real execution makes hypothesis runs more reliable; letting the model imagine the debugger output hurts. The model's own done signal separates good from bad runs.
numbers: Individual runs plausible: 73% with real debugger vs 63% with hallucinated debugger. A DONE-token prediction raised plausibility by 12.4 points with real execution but lowered it by 11 points when the debugger was hallucinated. Plausible patches without DONE were correct 82% of the time (the figure for DONE was cut off in the extracted text).
limits: Small benchmark (ARHE). A self-reported done token is partly a confidence signal.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 and 5: execution grounding is the active ingredient. A self-stated stop is informative only when it is grounded.

source: Spiess et al. (2024) Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code
finding: LLM confidence for code is poorly aligned with correctness across completion, synthesis and program repair. Reflective (ask-the-model) confidence is inconsistent. Platt rescaling helps.
numbers: Expected calibration error 0.09 to 0.73 across settings. Example: completions with average token probability above 90% passed tests only 52% of the time. Few-shot reflective prompt on GPT-3.5 code completion raised skill score from 0 to 0.15.
limits: Not fault localisation. Calibration of generated code, not of a location. Platt scaling needs labelled data.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: raw model confidence is a weak gate; a localisation-specific check (agreement across reruns or an execution check) is needed. AutoFL's 0.5 Spearman may not generalise.

source: Ehrlich et al. (2025) CodeMonkeys: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Software Engineering
finding: At a fixed cost, spending on more iterations per attempt or on more parallel attempts gives similar coverage after the first few iterations. So fresh samples are about as good as longer repair loops.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified: 57.4% resolved at about $2,300; coverage 69.8%; ensemble oracle coverage 80.8% with selection reaching 66.2%. Same-cost serial/parallel mixes give similar coverage.
limits: One system and benchmark; selection, not repair, is the bottleneck. No explicit re-localisation arm.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: resample versus continue is roughly a wash after a few iterations; consistent with Olausson's 1.05x. Re-localising has not been isolated.

source: Ehrlich et al. CodeMonkeys context stage (LLM reads every file)
finding: Letting an LLM scan each file and rank relevance puts the needed files into a 128k context for most issues at about 15% of total cost.
numbers: 92.6% of SWE-bench Verified instances had all gold files in context at the 128k limit; relevance scan 14.6% of spend (Table 1).
limits: Recall of gold-patch files only; alternative valid fixes in other files are not counted (authors' own footnote).
agent_relevance: Gap 8: brute-force test-free localisation is cheap and high-recall at file level; precision at line or symbol level remains open.

source: Liu et al. (2025) An Empirical Study on Failures in Automated Issue Solving
finding: Multi-file issues are where tools fail. Single-file issues are handled reasonably by all.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified (500). Overall: OpenHands 53.0%, Agentless 50.8%, Tools Claude 49.0%. Single-file 55-58% success for all; multi-file OpenHands 25.3%, with Agentless and Tools Claude lower (the text reports 18.3% and 11.3% in the sharpest bins).
limits: Three tools, one benchmark; file counts from the human patch. The exact bins for the 18.3% and 11.3% figures were not fully legible in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: multi-file faults are the clearest defeating class. The scaffold needs an explicit step to enumerate coupled files after the first fix.

source: Liu et al. failure taxonomy (150 failed instances)
finding: Pipelines fail mainly at localisation; agents fail mainly in iteration and validation. About 65% of root causes are flawed reasoning, such as fixating on issue keywords.
numbers: Manual analysis of 150 failures: 3 phases, 9 categories, 25 subcategories. Agentless: 51.3% of failed issues have a localisation error. Agentic: 49.1% (OpenHands) and 51.7% (Tools Claude) have iteration or validation errors. On easy tasks localisation errors are 41% (OpenHands) and 39% (Tools Claude). OpenHands iteration and validation failures rise from 27% (easy) to 64% (hard). Causes: flawed reasoning about 65%, knowledge deficiency about 25%, environment about 10%.
limits: Manual coding of 150 samples, two annotators; one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 7: when a patch fails, agents often fixate on the failing approach and lack self-correction, which supports a forced re-localisation step.

source: Liu et al. trajectory length and the Expert-Executor fix
finding: Successful runs end early. Failing runs run on in long tails, which suggests wasted exploration instead of useful checking.
numbers: OpenHands: 80% of successes within 25 rounds (median 16); 54 rounds needed to cover 80% of failures. Tools Claude: 80% of successes within 19 rounds (median 11). An added supervisor agent (Expert-Executor) resolved 22.2% of previously unsolved issues for a strong single agent.
limits: The supervisor result is on issues the base agent failed, so it is selected and may regress to the mean.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 6: a round cap near 25 plus an outside review step is a testable stop and re-plan rule.

source: Antoniades et al. (2025) SWE-Search: MCTS with backtracking for software agents
finding: Search with backtracking and a self-evaluating value function helped open-source agents. Scaling depth of search raised performance.
numbers: Abstract reports a 23% relative improvement across five models over agents without MCTS on SWE-bench.
limits: Only the abstract and framework description were read closely. Gains are relative; compute is larger than the baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: backtracking to an earlier state (a form of re-localising) helps, but compute is not matched.
